title: The Spice Islands
blurb: Cloves and nutmeg were once worth more than gold. How did tiny islands in Indonesia change the world?

chapters.title: The Smell of Fortune
chapters.text:
Open a kitchen cupboard and you may find small jars of cinnamon, pepper, cloves and nutmeg. We sprinkle them on food without thinking much about them. Yet for hundreds of years, these spices were among the most valuable goods in the world.

A spice is a part of a plant, such as a seed, a bark, a bud or a root, that we use to give flavour or fragrance. Before there were refrigerators, spices also helped people to hide the taste of food that was not fresh, and some were used as medicine.

Many spices come from the warm, wet lands near the equator. This is why the story of spices is so closely tied to the islands of Southeast Asia, where the sun is strong and the rain falls almost every month.

chapters.title: Islands of Spice
chapters.text:
Two of the most precious spices came from a handful of small islands in eastern Indonesia. Cloves grew naturally on a few islands in Maluku, such as Ternate and Tidore. These islands are the peaks of old volcanoes, and clove trees love the rich soil and the humid air. A clove is the dried flower bud of the tree, and it is picked before it opens.

Nutmeg grew on the Banda Islands, a tiny group of islands south of Maluku. The nutmeg tree gives two spices. The seed inside the fruit is nutmeg, and the red net that wraps around the seed is called mace.

For a long time, these trees did not grow in any other place on Earth. This made the spices rare, and rare things are expensive.

chapters.title: Along the Sea Roads
chapters.text:
The spices did not stay on the islands. Local traders carried them in small boats to ports on Java, Sumatra and Malay Peninsula. From there, merchants from India, Arabia and China bought them and shipped them west and north.

These voyages depended on the monsoon, a seasonal wind that changes direction every year. For about half the year, the wind blows from one side. Then it turns and blows from the opposite side. Sailors learned to travel with the wind in one direction and return with the wind on the way back.

By the time the spices reached Europe, they had passed through many hands. Each trader added a little to the price. A pinch of pepper in a London kitchen cost many times more than it did at the port where it was loaded.

chapters.title: Ships from Far Away
chapters.text:
In 1512, ships from Portugal reached the Banda Islands. The Portuguese wanted to buy spices directly, without the many traders in between. This was a big change, because Europeans had never before sailed so far east by sea, and the voyage took many months. Later, other European sailors followed. In 1602, a group of Dutch merchants started a powerful company called the Dutch East India Company, known as the VOC. It had its own ships, its own soldiers and its own rules.

The VOC wanted to control the whole spice trade. It forced the local people to sell only to the company, at low prices. It also fought wars to take control of the islands. Life on the islands changed for ever, and many people suffered because of this. Their story is an important part of Indonesian history.

chapters.title: A Tiny Island and a Big Deal
chapters.text:
In the 1600s, the Netherlands and England competed for the spice islands. One of the places they fought over was Run, a very small island in the Banda group. Run was only about three kilometres long, but it was covered in nutmeg trees.

In 1667, the two countries signed an agreement called the Treaty of Breda. England gave up its claim to Run. In exchange, the Dutch gave up their claim to a place in North America called New Amsterdam. Today, New Amsterdam is known as New York City, and the part where the Dutch had settled is called Manhattan. It is one of the busiest places in the world.

Back then, people thought the Dutch had made a good bargain. A tiny island with nutmeg trees seemed more valuable than a big piece of land.

chapters.title: Spices Today
chapters.text:
The Dutch tried to keep the nutmeg and clove trees only on their own islands. But it was not possible to guard every seed for ever. In the 1700s and 1800s, seedlings were taken to other warm places, such as Mauritius, the Caribbean and Zanzibar. Once the trees grew elsewhere, spices became cheaper.

Today, spices are not treasures but everyday goods. Indonesia is still one of the biggest producers of nutmeg and cloves in the world. In Indonesian kitchens, people use cloves, nutmeg and many other spices in dishes such as soto and rendang.

Clove oil is still used in some medicines for the teeth, too. The story of spices reminds us that things that seem small can have a big influence on history. It began with a tiny bud and a small island.
